mis.m: Thinks 1,045 can only be 1 thousand, 0 hundreds, 4 tens and 5 ones, and says '10 hundreds and 45 ones' is a different number.
mis.why: Students have practiced one standard way to build a number and do not yet see that trading keeps the value the same.
mis.fix: Build 1,045 with base-ten blocks, then trade the thousand cube for 10 flats while the class counts on; ask, 'Did the number change?'

mis.m: Builds 306 as 3 flats and 6 rods because the 6 is 'next to' the 3.
mis.why: Students read digits left to right without attending to the zero holding the tens place.
mis.fix: Use a place value mat with labeled columns and have students place blocks column by column, saying 'zero tens' out loud.

mis.m: When decomposing 152 as 14 tens and 12 ones, writes 140 + 12 = 1,412 or loses track of the tens.
mis.why: Students are unsure how many ones are in a group of tens once there are more than 9 tens.
mis.fix: Bundle 14 rods into 1 flat and 4 rods on the mat, then record each version as a sum so students see 100 + 50 + 2 = 140 + 12.

cra.c: Students build a number up to 1,200 with base-ten blocks or place value disks on a place value mat, then trade one hundred for 10 tens or one ten for 10 ones to make a second way.
cra.r: Students sketch quick pictures (squares for hundreds, sticks for tens, dots for ones) for two different builds of the same number and label each part.
cra.a: Students write each build as a sum, such as 1,000 + 100 + 30 + 4 and 1,000 + 13 tens + 4, pointing to the matching part of their sketch.
cra.look: Partners trade blocks on mats, sketch two different builds of one number, and explain why both still show the same amount.

assess: How did you build this number a second way?
What did you trade, and why is the number still the same?
advance: Can you show 1,200 using no thousand cube at all?
How many different ways can you build 250 using only hundreds and tens?

assess: Which part of your sketch shows the tens?
How many ones would you have if you broke this ten apart?
advance: Can you trade one more hundred and show the new way?
How would you write your new build as a sum?

assess: Point to the hundreds on your mat.
How many tens are in one flat?
advance: What happens if we trade this flat for rods? Count them with me.
Is 10 tens the same as 1 hundred? Show me.
support: Start with numbers under 200 and only one trade at a time.
Give a mat with picture labels for hundreds, tens and ones.

stems: I built ___ with ___ hundreds, ___ tens and ___ ones.
I agree with ___ because both builds show ___.
d: Use concrete and pictorial models to compose and decompose numbers up to 1,200 in more than one way as a sum of so many thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones.

mis.m: Writes 'four hundred six' as 4006 or 46.
mis.why: Students write each spoken part as its own number instead of thinking about place value.
mis.fix: Have students place the number on a place value chart first, then write it in standard form, checking that the hundreds digit is in the third place from the right.

mis.m: Writes 1,050 in expanded notation as 1,000 + 0 + 50 + 0 or as 1 + 0 + 5 + 0.
mis.why: Students list digits instead of the value of each digit and are unsure how to handle zeros.
mis.fix: Build the number with base-ten blocks and ask, 'What is this digit worth?' for each place; cross out parts worth zero.

mis.m: Writes 'three hundred and twelve' in word form, adding 'and', or spells 'forty' as 'fourty'.
mis.why: Spoken habits carry into writing and number words are not on display.
mis.fix: Keep a number word wall and practice saying numbers without 'and' while pointing to each place on the chart.

cra.c: Students build a number with base-ten blocks or place value disks, then match it to cards showing its standard, word and expanded forms.
cra.r: Students fill in a four-way graphic organizer: quick picture, standard form, word form and expanded notation for the same number.
cra.a: Students convert between forms without models, such as writing 900 + 80 + 7 as 987 and in words, and explain how each digit's value shows up.
cra.look: Students hold up matching cards for one number in all three forms and point to the blocks that show each part.

assess: How did you know what to write for the tens?
Why is there a zero in your standard form?
advance: How would the expanded notation change if the tens digit became zero?
Can you write 1,000 + 200 in standard form and in words?

assess: Which blocks match the 600 in your expanded notation?
How did you write this number in words?
advance: What number is 10 more? Write it in all three forms.
What would change if you added one more hundred?

assess: Point to the digit in the hundreds place.
What is this 4 worth?
advance: Can you say the number as you point to each block?
What goes in the tens place when there are no tens?
support: Use a place value chart with columns labeled hundreds, tens, ones.
Give a word bank with number words from one to twenty and the tens words.

stems: I wrote a zero because there are no ___.
d: Use standard, word, and expanded forms to represent numbers up to 1,200.

mis.m: When asked for a number greater than 489, writes 480 because it 'has an 8' or shares digits.
mis.why: Students focus on familiar digits rather than comparing place values.
mis.fix: Build both numbers with base-ten blocks and ask, 'Which one has more hundreds? If the same, which has more tens?'

mis.m: Gives only the next counting number, 490, and says no other number can be greater.
mis.why: Students think 'greater than' means 'one more than'.
mis.fix: Use an open number line and ask students to mark three different numbers that land to the right of 489.

mis.m: Writes a number less than 1,005 as 1,004 but then 999 seems 'bigger' because it has more nines.
mis.why: Students compare by the size of digits instead of the number of places.
mis.fix: Build 999 and 1,005 with blocks and line them up; ask which pile has a thousand.

cra.c: Students build a given number with base-ten blocks, then add or remove blocks to create a number that is greater or less and explain what they changed.
cra.r: Students mark the given number on an open number line and place their new numbers to the right for greater and to the left for less.
cra.a: Students write several numbers greater and less than a given number and use place value words to tell why each works.
cra.look: Students change blocks on a mat and place sticky notes on a class number line to show greater and less numbers.

assess: How do you know your number is greater?
What place did you change to make it less?
advance: Can you find a number that is greater but has fewer ones?
What is the greatest number you can make that is still less than 600?

assess: Where did you put your number on the number line?
What did you add to your blocks?
advance: Can you find a number greater by changing only the hundreds?
Is there a number between your two numbers?

assess: Show me the given number with blocks.
Which is more, this pile or that pile?
advance: If I add one flat, is the number greater or less?
Can you take away a rod and tell me the new number?
support: Start with numbers under 100 before moving to hundreds.
Give a number line with the given number already marked.

stems: A number greater than ___ is ___ because ___.
A number less than ___ is ___ because ___.
My number is to the ___ on the number line.
d: Generate a number that is greater than or less than a given whole number up to 1,200.

mis.m: Says 98 is greater than 102 because 9 is bigger than 1.
mis.why: Students compare the first digits they see without lining up places.
mis.fix: Line up the numbers on a place value chart and compare hundreds first; build both with base-ten blocks.

mis.m: Reverses the symbols, writing 345 > 543.
mis.why: Students memorize 'alligator' tricks without connecting the symbol to the words 'greater than' and 'less than'.
mis.fix: Have students read each statement aloud left to right, 'three hundred forty-five is less than five hundred forty-three', and check with blocks.

mis.m: Orders 1,020, 1,002 and 1,200 by the last digits, putting 1,002 last.
mis.why: Students compare the ones digit first because it is the 'end' of the number.
mis.fix: Have students circle the first place where the digits differ and compare only that place.

cra.c: Students build two or three numbers with base-ten blocks side by side and compare thousands, then hundreds, then tens, then ones.
cra.r: Students place numbers on a place value chart or an open number line and order them from least to greatest.
cra.a: Students write comparison statements with >, < or = and in words, and order sets of three numbers.
cra.look: Students line up blocks or chart rows, circle the deciding place, and read comparison statements aloud.

assess: Which place helped you decide?
How do you know these numbers are equal?
advance: Can you change one digit to make the statement true the other way?
How would you order four numbers that all have the same hundreds?

assess: Which number is farther right on your number line?
Where do the digits first become different?
advance: Can you write the comparison in words too?
Where would 1,100 fit in your order?

assess: Which pile has more hundreds?
Read this symbol to me.
advance: Is 120 greater or less than 210? Show me with blocks.
Which number would come first if we count up?
support: Compare two-digit numbers first, then add hundreds.
Give a symbol card with 'greater than' and 'less than' written under each symbol.

stems: From least to greatest, the order is ___.
d: Use place value to compare and order whole numbers up to 1,200 using comparative language, numbers, and symbols (>, <, or =).

mis.m: Places 75 exactly halfway between 0 and 100 but then places 30 near 70 because the spacing is uneven.
mis.why: Students do not use benchmark numbers to keep distances consistent.
mis.fix: Have students mark benchmarks like 50 first, then place other numbers relative to them.

mis.m: Starts every open number line at 0 even when the number is 840.
mis.why: Students have mostly seen number lines starting at zero.
mis.fix: Show that an open number line can start at any helpful number, such as 800 to 900, and mark the endpoints first.

mis.m: Places 460 between 400 and 450 because 6 is 'small'.
mis.why: Students do not think about where the tens place puts the number.
mis.fix: Count by tens from 400 on the line, marking each jump, until students reach 460.

cra.c: Students stand on a floor number line made with tape and clothespins on a string to place number cards between benchmark cards.
cra.r: Students draw open number lines, choose endpoints, mark a benchmark in the middle and place the given number.
cra.a: Students explain the position using numbers: '460 is 60 more than 400 and 40 less than 500, so it is closer to 500.'
cra.look: Students choose endpoints, mark benchmarks and explain why their number is closer to one end.

assess: How did you choose your endpoints?
Why did you put the number there and not closer to the other end?
advance: Where would a number 10 more go?
Can you use different endpoints and still place it correctly?

assess: What benchmark did you mark first?
Is your number closer to the start or the end?
advance: Where would the halfway number go?
Can you place two more numbers on the same line?

assess: Point to the start of your line.
Is 460 more or less than 450?
advance: Count by tens with me from 400. Where do we stop?
Which end is your number closer to?
support: Give number lines with endpoints already labeled.
Use a clothesline with tens already clipped on.

stems: I started my number line at ___ and ended at ___.
d: Locate the position of a given whole number on an open number line.

mis.m: Counts tick marks instead of spaces and names the point 1 too many.
mis.why: Students count the starting tick as a jump.
mis.fix: Have students put a finger on the start and count each hop between ticks, saying the number as they land.

mis.m: Assumes every tick mark counts by 1 even when the labels show 0, 10, 20.
mis.why: Students do not look at labels to find the jump size.
mis.fix: Ask, 'What are we counting by?' and have students skip count aloud between two labeled ticks before naming the point.

mis.m: Names the point as the closest label rather than the exact value.
mis.why: Students round to a known number instead of counting on.
mis.fix: Have students count on from the nearest label to the exact tick and write the number above it.

cra.c: Students hop a token along a floor number line or a meter stick labeled by ones, fives or tens, saying the number at each landing.
cra.r: Students read number lines with some labels missing, write the jump size, and fill in the number for each marked point.
cra.a: Students name the point and write the counting pattern that proves it, such as 300, 310, 320, 330.
cra.look: Students skip count aloud while tracing the line and write the missing numbers above the marked points.

assess: What are the jumps on this number line?
How did you know the point was 530?
advance: What number would be two ticks to the right?
How would the point change if each jump were 5?

assess: Which label did you start counting from?
How many jumps did you make?
advance: Can you name the point halfway between these two labels?
What if we count backward from the next label?

assess: Put your finger on 0. Count the hops with me.
What number is on this tick?
advance: Do the numbers go up by 1 or by 10 here?
What comes after 20 when we count by tens?
support: Start with number lines labeled at every tick, then remove some labels.
Use a skip counting chart beside the number line.

stems: I started at ___ and counted ___ jumps.
d: Name the whole number that corresponds to a specific point on a number line.

mis.m: Cuts a rectangle into 4 pieces of different sizes and calls each piece 'one-fourth'.
mis.why: Students count pieces without checking that the parts are equal.
mis.fix: Fold paper shapes so parts match exactly, and ask, 'Are all the parts the same size?' before naming them.

mis.m: Calls each part of a shape cut into 8 equal parts 'one-eight' or 'one-eighteen'.
mis.why: The fraction words are new and sound like counting numbers.
mis.fix: Post a word card for halves, fourths and eighths with a folded paper example, and have students say the name as they touch each part.

mis.m: Thinks a fourth must be a square corner piece and does not accept four equal strips.
mis.why: Students have seen only one way to partition each shape.
mis.fix: Partition the same square two ways, into four strips and four small squares, and lay pieces on top of each other to compare.

cra.c: Students fold paper circles, squares and rectangles, cut sandwiches of paper or clay strips, and use fraction pieces into halves, fourths and eighths.
cra.r: Students draw lines to partition shapes into equal parts and label each part with a word, such as 'one-fourth'.
cra.a: Students name the parts in words and tell how many equal parts make the whole: 'There are 8 equal parts. Each part is one-eighth.'
cra.look: Students fold and check that parts match, and say fraction words while touching each part.

assess: How do you know the parts are equal?
What is the name of each part?
advance: Can you partition the same shape into fourths a different way?
How could you turn halves into fourths?

assess: How many equal parts did you draw?
Which word names one of these parts?
advance: What would happen if you folded it one more time?
Can you show eighths on a rectangle?

assess: Show me one half.
Are these two parts the same size?
advance: Fold this square so both sides match. What did you make?
Touch each part and say its name with me.
support: Use pre-folded shapes and let students trace the fold lines.
Give a picture word card for halves, fourths and eighths.

stems: I cut the shape into ___ equal parts.
d: Partition objects into equal parts and name the parts, including halves, fourths, and eighths, using words.

mis.m: Says one-eighth is bigger than one-fourth because 8 is bigger than 4.
mis.why: Students apply whole-number thinking to fraction names.
mis.fix: Cut two same-size paper strips into fourths and eighths and lay one part of each side by side.

mis.m: Compares one-half of a small cracker with one-fourth of a large pizza to say fourths can be bigger.
mis.why: Students do not hold the whole the same when comparing parts.
mis.fix: Insist on the same-size whole for every comparison and ask, 'Are the wholes the same?'

mis.m: Believes more parts means more to eat.
mis.why: Students focus on the number of pieces, not their size.
mis.fix: Share one paper cookie among 2 friends and another same-size cookie among 8 friends, and ask who gets the bigger piece.

cra.c: Students fold same-size paper strips into halves, fourths and eighths and stack the strips to compare one part of each.
cra.r: Students draw same-size rectangles partitioned into halves, fourths and eighths and shade one part of each.
cra.a: Students state the rule in words: 'The more equal parts in a whole, the smaller each part is.'
cra.look: Students line up folded strips that start the same length and point to the larger and smaller parts.

assess: Why is one-half bigger than one-eighth?
What happens to each part when you fold again?
advance: If you shared a pizza with more friends, would your piece get bigger or smaller? Why?
Would this rule work for any whole? Show me.

assess: Are your strips the same size to start?
Which strip has the most parts?
advance: Which part would be smaller, one-fourth or one-eighth? Prove it with strips.
What if you folded the eighths strip one more time?

assess: Which piece is bigger?
How many parts are in this strip?
advance: Lay these two pieces on top of each other. What do you see?
If I share with more friends, do I get more or less?
support: Start with halves and fourths only.
Provide strips already folded and cut.

stems: One-___ is bigger than one-___ because ___.
The more parts, the ___ each part is.
The fewer parts, the ___ each part is.
I know because my strips show ___.
d: Explain that the more fractional parts used to make a whole, the smaller the part; and the fewer the fractional parts, the larger the part.

mis.m: Counts 'one-fourth, two-fourths, three-fourths, four-fourths, five-fourths' but says five-fourths is less than one whole.
mis.why: Students think fractions are always less than one.
mis.fix: Count fourths onto a whole paper circle until it is full, then start a second circle and keep counting.

mis.m: Counts fraction pieces as whole numbers: 'one, two, three' instead of 'one-half, two-halves, three-halves'.
mis.why: The counting habit from whole numbers takes over.
mis.fix: Have students say the unit name every time they place a piece, and write the count under each piece in words.

mis.m: Says it takes 4 pieces to make a whole for any fraction.
mis.why: Students remember one example rather than the number of parts.
mis.fix: Ask, 'How many parts does the whole have?' and build a whole with halves, fourths and eighths side by side.

cra.c: Students place fraction pieces or fold paper circles, counting each piece aloud by its name, and keep going past one whole onto a second whole.
cra.r: Students draw two whole shapes partitioned into fourths or eighths and shade and count parts beyond one whole.
cra.a: Students tell the count in words and how many parts make one whole: 'Six-fourths is one whole and two more fourths.'
cra.look: Students count fraction pieces aloud by name and stop to say when they reach one whole.

assess: How many fourths make one whole?
How do you know you have more than one whole?
advance: How many eighths are in two wholes?
Is ten-eighths more or less than one whole? Explain.

assess: Show me where your first whole is full.
How many pieces are left over?
advance: How many more pieces do you need to make two wholes?
Can you count the same amount using halves?

assess: Count these pieces with me using their name.
Is this circle full?
advance: How many halves fill this circle?
If I add one more half, do we have more than one whole?
support: Start with halves before fourths and eighths.
Use a whole outline mat to place pieces on.

stems: It takes ___ ___ to make one whole.
I have one whole and ___ more.
This is more than one whole because ___.
d: Use concrete models to count fractional parts beyond one whole using words and recognize how many parts it takes to equal one whole.

mis.m: Accepts a shape split into 4 unequal pieces as an example of fourths.
mis.why: Students count parts without checking size.
mis.fix: Cut the parts out and stack them; if they do not match, the shape is a non-example.

mis.m: Rejects a shape split into 2 equal triangles as a half because the parts 'don't look like halves'.
mis.why: Students expect halves to be split down the middle in a straight vertical line.
mis.fix: Show many ways to split the same square in half, including diagonal lines, and test by folding.

mis.m: Calls a shape with 8 parts eighths even when some parts are left over or the whole is not used.
mis.why: Students do not check that the equal parts make the whole.
mis.fix: Have students trace each part and check that all parts together fill the whole shape.

cra.c: Students sort paper shapes into 'equal parts' and 'not equal parts' piles by folding and stacking cut pieces.
cra.r: Students sort picture cards into examples and non-examples of halves, fourths and eighths on a T-chart.
cra.a: Students explain each choice in words: 'This is not fourths because the parts are not the same size.'
cra.look: Students fold, stack and sort shapes, and tell a partner why a shape is or is not an example.

assess: Why is this a non-example?
How did you check the parts are equal?
advance: Can you draw a non-example of eighths that has 8 parts?
Can you make two different-looking examples of halves?

assess: Which pile did you put this in?
Did you fold it to check?
advance: Can you fix this non-example so it shows fourths?
Draw one more example and one more non-example.

assess: Are these parts the same size?
How many parts are there?
advance: Fold it. Do the parts match?
Is this halves, yes or no?
support: Start with halves only.
Give shapes that can be cut out and stacked.

stems: This is an example of ___ because ___.
This is not an example because ___.
d: Identify examples and non-examples of halves, fourths, and eighths.

mis.m: Counts on fingers for 8 + 7 and loses track, answering 14.
mis.why: Students rely on counting by ones instead of using a strategy.
mis.fix: Teach make-a-ten on a ten frame: move 2 counters from 7 to fill the 8, making 10 + 5.

mis.m: Solves 13 − 9 by counting back and lands on 5.
mis.why: Students count the starting number as the first step back.
mis.fix: Use think-addition: '9 plus what makes 13?' and count up on a number line from 9.

mis.m: Knows 6 + 4 = 10 but does not connect it to 10 − 4 = 6.
mis.why: Facts are memorized separately without seeing fact families.
mis.fix: Use a number bond or part-part-whole mat and write all four related facts.

cra.c: Students use double ten frames, counters and connecting cubes to make a ten and find doubles and near doubles.
cra.r: Students use number bonds, ten frame pictures and number lines to show the strategy they used for a fact.
cra.a: Students recall facts quickly in games and fact family lists, and name the strategy that helps for harder facts.
cra.look: Students play quick fact games, name strategies like make-a-ten or doubles, and check with ten frames.

assess: What strategy did you use for 9 + 6?
How does knowing 7 + 7 help with 7 + 8?
advance: Which facts are hardest for you, and what strategy could help?
How can an addition fact help you subtract?

assess: Show me how you made a ten.
What fact family does this belong to?
advance: Can you solve 17 − 8 by thinking addition?
Which double is close to 6 + 7?

assess: Fill this ten frame. How many more to 10?
What is 5 + 5?
advance: If 5 + 5 is 10, what is 5 + 6?
Use the counters. How many in all?
support: Practice a small set of facts with ten frames before mixing.
Give a fact strategy card with a ten frame picture.

d: Recall basic facts to add and subtract within 20 with automaticity.

mis.m: Lines up 46 + 7 + 23 with the 7 under the 4, getting a wrong total.
mis.why: Students do not line up numbers by place value.
mis.fix: Build each number with base-ten blocks on a place value mat and record in columns labeled tens and ones.

mis.m: Subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in each place: 52 − 38 = 26.
mis.why: Students avoid regrouping by flipping the digits.
mis.fix: Build 52 with blocks, try to take away 8 ones, and trade a ten for 10 ones before subtracting.

mis.m: Adds four two-digit numbers one at a time and loses partial sums.
mis.why: Students do not look for friendly pairs or keep a record.
mis.fix: Show how to group numbers that make tens first, like 25 + 15, and record partial sums on paper.

cra.c: Students build each addend with base-ten blocks or place value disks and combine tens and ones, trading 10 ones for a ten when needed.
cra.r: Students use open number lines to jump by tens and ones and record partial sums or regrouping in a place value chart.
cra.a: Students use mental strategies and algorithms, writing each step and explaining it with place value words.
cra.look: Students trade blocks, jump on open number lines, and explain why they regrouped.

assess: How did you decide which numbers to add first?
Why did you need to regroup?
advance: Is there a faster way to add these four numbers? Show me.
How could you check your subtraction with addition?

assess: Show me your jumps on the number line.
What did you trade?
advance: Can you solve it another way?
Which numbers make a ten together?

assess: Show 52 with blocks.
Do you have enough ones to take away 8?
advance: What can you trade so you have more ones?
How many tens now?
support: Start with two addends, then add more.
Give a place value mat with ten frames for ones.

d: Add up to four two-digit numbers and subtract two-digit numbers using mental strategies and algorithms based on knowledge of place value and properties of operations.

mis.m: Adds every number in the problem because of the word 'more', even in a compare problem asking how many more.
mis.why: Students hunt for key words instead of picturing the story.
mis.fix: Have students act out or draw a strip diagram before choosing to add or subtract.

mis.m: Solves only the first step of a two-step problem and stops.
mis.why: Students do not reread the question after the first answer.
mis.fix: Have students underline the question and check off each part of the story as they use it.

mis.m: Lines up 345 + 23 with the 2 under the 3 and gets 575 instead of 368.
mis.why: Students line up numbers on the left like words instead of by place value.
mis.fix: Build both numbers with place value disks on a hundreds, tens and ones mat and record in labeled columns.

cra.c: Students act out stories with counters or base-ten blocks and use place value disks for larger numbers.
cra.r: Students draw strip diagrams to show the parts and whole or the comparison, and use open number lines to solve.
cra.a: Students write a number sentence for each step and answer in a complete sentence with units.
cra.look: Students draw strip diagrams, label the known and unknown parts, and explain why they added or subtracted.

assess: How did your strip diagram help you decide to add or subtract?
How do you know your answer makes sense?
advance: What if the story had one more step? What would you do?
Can you solve it a different way and get the same answer?

assess: Which part of the strip diagram is unknown?
What is the first step?
advance: What is the second step?
Can you check your answer with the other operation?

assess: Tell me the story in your own words.
Show me the parts with blocks.
advance: Are we putting together or taking apart?
Which part is missing?
support: Use smaller numbers first with the same story.
Give a strip diagram with labels already drawn.

d: Solve one-step and multi-step word problems involving addition and subtraction within 1,000 using a variety of strategies based on place value, including algorithms.

mis.m: For 450 − 120 = ___, writes a story about putting 450 and 120 together.
mis.why: Students write any story with the numbers without matching the action.
mis.fix: Have students act out the number sentence with blocks first, then tell what happened.

mis.m: Writes a story with no question, so there is nothing to solve.
mis.why: Students think a story problem is just a story.
mis.fix: Give a frame with a 'question' line and ask partners to answer each other's question.

mis.m: Writes a story where the numbers do not make sense, like 600 kids in a car.
mis.why: Students focus on numbers and not on real contexts.
mis.fix: Brainstorm a list of things that come in hundreds, like pages, stickers or points.

cra.c: Students use base-ten blocks to act out the number sentence, then tell a story that matches the action.
cra.r: Students draw a strip diagram for the number sentence and label it with story words.
cra.a: Students write the story problem, solve it, and check that the number sentence matches.
cra.look: Students trade stories, solve partner problems, and check that each story matches the number sentence.

assess: How does your story match the number sentence?
What is the question in your story?
advance: Can you write a different kind of story for the same number sentence?
How would your story change if it were addition?

assess: What does each part of your strip diagram stand for?
What is happening in your story?
advance: Can your partner solve your story?
Can you change the story so the unknown is at the start?

assess: What are we doing with these numbers, adding or taking away?
What is your story about?
advance: Can you show it with blocks?
What question can you ask?
support: Use a story frame with blanks to fill in.
Start with smaller numbers.

stems: I can change my story by ___.
d: Generate and solve problem situations for a given mathematical number sentence involving addition and subtraction of whole numbers within 1,000.

mis.m: Counts each coin as 1 cent or by its size, saying a dime is worth less than a nickel.
mis.why: Students link value to coin size.
mis.fix: Use a coin chart with pictures and values, and sort real or play coins by value.

mis.m: Counts a quarter, dime and nickel as 25, 26, 27.
mis.why: Students switch to counting by ones after the first coin.
mis.fix: Model counting on: start with the biggest value, then count on by tens, fives and ones.

mis.m: Has 4 quarters or 10 dimes and does not recognize the collection is exactly one dollar.
mis.why: Students count to 100 cents but have not linked 100 cents to one dollar.
mis.fix: Build 100 cents several ways with play coins and trade each collection for a dollar bill while saying '100 cents is one dollar'.

cra.c: Students sort a handful of play coins by value, line them up from greatest to least, and count on: 25, 35, 45, 50, 51.
cra.r: Students draw the coins and show the counting-on jumps on an open number line or hundred chart, labeling each jump with the coin.
cra.a: Students write the total in cents and the counting sequence they used, and compare two collections to tell which is worth more.
cra.look: Students sort coins from greatest to least value, count on aloud by different amounts, and record each total.

assess: How did you count these coins?
Why did you start with the quarter?
advance: Can you make the same amount a different way?
How many more cents to make a dollar?

assess: Show me your jumps on the number line.
What is each coin worth?
advance: What if we add one more dime?
Can you make 50 cents with fewer coins?

assess: Which coin is this?
How much is a dime worth?
advance: Count on from 25 by fives with me.
Do we have a dollar yet?
support: Use only dimes and pennies first.
Give a coin value chart.

stems: I can make ___ another way by ___.
d: Determine the value of a collection of coins up to one dollar.

mis.m: Writes 45 cents as $45 or 45$.
mis.why: Students use the dollar sign for any money amount.
mis.fix: Show 45 cents and $45 side by side with play money, and ask which one buys a toy and which buys a gum ball.

mis.m: Writes 7 cents as $0.7.
mis.why: Students do not know the decimal point needs two places for cents.
mis.fix: Use a money place chart with dollars, a decimal point and two cents boxes, and write 0 in the dimes box.

mis.m: Uses both symbols together, like $0.35¢.
mis.why: Students think more symbols make the amount clearer.
mis.fix: Post two examples, 35¢ and $0.35, and say they mean the same; choose one symbol, not both.

cra.c: Students count a collection of play coins and record the value two ways on a money mat: with the cent symbol and with the dollar sign and decimal point.
cra.r: Students draw coin collections and label the total on a price tag, then match tags that show the same value in different notation.
cra.a: Students write amounts like 68¢ and $0.68 and explain that the decimal point separates dollars from cents.
cra.look: Students count coins, write price tags in both notations, and match equal amounts.

assess: Why does $0.35 have a zero before the decimal point?
How are 35¢ and $0.35 the same?
advance: How would you write one dollar both ways?
How would you write 9 cents with the dollar sign?

assess: Where does the decimal point go?
What symbol did you use?
advance: Can you write this amount the other way?
Which price tag matches 50¢?

assess: Point to the cent symbol.
How many cents is this?
advance: Let's write it with the cent symbol first.
Do we have any whole dollars?
support: Give a money mat with boxes for each digit.
Use collections under 50 cents first.

stems: I can write it as ___ or ___.
d: Use the cent symbol, dollar sign, and the decimal point to name the value of a collection of coins.

mis.m: Makes groups of different sizes and calls it 3 groups of 4.
mis.why: Students focus on the number of groups and not on equal groups.
mis.fix: Have students check every group by counting and fix any group that is not the same.

mis.m: Counts the total by ones and cannot tell how many groups or how many in each group.
mis.why: Students do not yet see the structure of equal groups.
mis.fix: Use egg cartons or paper plates and ask students to say '3 groups of 4' before counting.

mis.m: Confuses 4 groups of 3 with 3 groups of 4 in a story.
mis.why: Students do not match the story context to the groups.
mis.fix: Act out the story with real objects and label the groups with the story words.

cra.c: Students join equal sets of counters, cubes or real objects on plates or cups to act out stories like '4 bags with 5 apples each'.
cra.r: Students draw equal groups, arrays or skip counting jumps on a number line to show the story.
cra.a: Students describe the situation using 'groups of' and skip count to find the total, such as '4 groups of 5 is 5, 10, 15, 20'.
cra.look: Students build equal groups, skip count aloud and tell the story using 'groups of' language.

assess: How do you know the groups are equal?
How many groups and how many in each?
advance: What if we added one more group?
Can you write your own story for 5 groups of 2?

assess: Show me the groups in your drawing.
What did you skip count by?
advance: Can you show this story as an array?
How would the total change with 4 in each group?

assess: How many in this group?
Are all the groups the same?
advance: Let's count each group together.
Can you put 2 in each cup?
support: Use small numbers like 2 groups of 3.
Give cups or plates to hold each group.

d: Model, create, and describe contextual multiplication situations in which equivalent sets of concrete objects are joined.

mis.m: Shares 12 counters into 3 groups but ends with 5, 4 and 3.
mis.why: Students hand out objects without checking for equal sets.
mis.fix: Use a 'one for you, one for you' dealing routine and check each group before answering.

mis.m: Confuses 'how many groups' with 'how many in each group'.
mis.why: Students hear division stories but do not track what is unknown.
mis.fix: Act out both kinds of stories and ask, 'Do we know the number of groups or the number in each group?'

mis.m: Leaves extra objects and calls the answer correct.
mis.why: Students do not notice leftovers or think they do not matter.
mis.fix: Ask, 'Did every object get used? Are the groups still equal?' and choose numbers that share evenly.

cra.c: Students separate a set of counters, cubes or snacks into equal groups using plates or cups to act out sharing stories.
cra.r: Students draw circles for groups and deal dots into each one, or draw a strip diagram split into equal parts.
cra.a: Students describe the situation: '15 crayons shared into 3 boxes is 5 crayons in each box.'
cra.look: Students deal objects one at a time into groups and check that each group is equal.

assess: How did you share the objects?
How do you know each group got the same amount?
advance: What if there were 2 more objects?
Can you share the same number into a different number of groups?

assess: Show me how many in each group.
Did you use all the objects?
advance: What if we made groups of 4 instead?
Can you draw the story another way?

assess: Give one to each plate.
How many are on this plate?
advance: Are the plates the same?
Do we have any left?
support: Use small numbers like 6 shared by 2.
Provide plates or cups to sort into.

d: Model, create, and describe contextual division situations in which a set of concrete objects is separated into equivalent sets.

mis.m: Says 23 is even because 2 is an even digit, or says 30 is odd because 3 is odd.
mis.why: Students look at the tens digit instead of pairing the objects.
mis.fix: Build the number with counters in two rows and check whether any counter is left without a partner.

mis.m: Pairs objects quickly, misses one, and calls an odd number even.
mis.why: Students pair loosely without a way to keep track.
mis.fix: Use a two-row pairing mat or ten frames and have students touch each pair as they count.

mis.m: Thinks 0 is neither even nor odd, or that even means 'small' and odd means 'big'.
mis.why: The words are new and students link them to everyday meanings.
mis.fix: Show cube trains for 0, 2, 4, 6 side by side and say, 'Every cube has a partner, so it is even.'

cra.c: Students pair counters, linking cubes or even classmates for numbers up to 40, building two equal rows and checking for a leftover.
cra.r: Students draw dots in pairs or fill ten frames in pairs and circle any leftover dot.
cra.a: Students state whether a number is even or odd and explain using pairs: '27 is odd because 13 pairs leave 1 left over.'
cra.look: Students build two equal rows, point to any leftover, and explain their choice using the word pairs.

assess: How do you know 18 is even?
What happened when you paired 15?
advance: What do you notice about the ones digit of the even numbers you found?
If you add 1 to an even number, is the new number even or odd? Prove it.

assess: Show me your pairs in two rows.
Is there a leftover?
advance: Can you predict if 25 is even or odd before you pair it?
What about 30 and 31?

assess: Put these counters in pairs.
Does every counter have a partner?
advance: Touch each pair with me. Is there one left?
If I add one more counter, does it get a partner?
support: Start with numbers up to 10, then go to 20 and 40.
Give a two-row pairing mat.

d: Determine whether a number up to 40 is even or odd using pairings of objects to represent the number.

mis.m: Writes 10 more than 345 as 346 or 445.
mis.why: Students change the ones or hundreds place instead of the tens.
mis.fix: Build 345 with base-ten blocks, add exactly one rod, and ask, 'Which digit changed? Which stayed the same?'

mis.m: Writes 100 less than 1,050 as 1,040 or 50.
mis.why: Students are unsure how to take a hundred when the hundreds digit is zero.
mis.fix: Use a place value mat to trade the thousand cube for 10 flats, then take one flat away and count what is left.

mis.m: Writes 10 more than 495 as 4,105.
mis.why: Students write ten tens as '10' in the tens place instead of regrouping.
mis.fix: Build 495, add a rod, and trade 10 rods for a flat so students see 505.

cra.c: Students build a number up to 1,200 with base-ten blocks or place value disks and add or remove one rod or one flat, trading when needed.
cra.r: Students use a hundred chart or an open number line to show jumps of 10 or 100, writing the new number at each landing.
cra.a: Students write the new number and the pattern, such as 362, 372, 382, and explain which digit changed and why.
cra.look: Students add or remove one rod or flat, read the new number, and name the digit that changed.

assess: Which digit changed when you added 10? Why?
Why didn't the ones digit change?
advance: What is 100 more than 1,100?
What happens when you add 10 to 395? Show it with blocks.

assess: Show me the jump on your number line.
What did you add to your blocks?
advance: Can you find 10 less too?
What about 100 less? Which digit changes now?

assess: Show me one rod. How much is it worth?
Which block is worth 100?
advance: Add one rod. What is the new number?
Count the rods with me. Which place changed?
support: Start with numbers under 100 on a hundred chart.
Give a place value mat with labeled columns.

stems: The other digits stayed the same because ___.
d: Use an understanding of place value to determine the number that is 10 or 100 more or less than a given number up to 1,200.

mis.m: For '___ + 7 = 15', adds 7 and 15 to get 22.
mis.why: Students add all the numbers they see without thinking about the story.
mis.fix: Act out the story with counters in a cup, keep the start amount hidden, and ask, 'How many were there at first?'

mis.m: Expects the unknown to always be the answer at the end, and is stuck when the change or start is missing.
mis.why: Students have mostly seen result-unknown problems.
mis.fix: Use a strip diagram with a question mark in different places and practice result-, change- and start-unknown stories side by side.

mis.m: Subtracts in a compare story when the bigger amount is unknown.
mis.why: Students hear 'fewer' or 'less' and choose subtraction as a key word.
mis.fix: Draw two strips for a compare problem, label which is longer, and decide whether to find the whole or a part.

cra.c: Students act out stories with counters and cups, hiding the unknown amount under a cup until they solve it.
cra.r: Students draw strip diagrams with a question mark in the unknown spot, then solve using an open number line by counting up or back.
cra.a: Students write a number sentence with a box or blank for the unknown, such as ___ − 12 = 30, solve it, and check with the related fact.
cra.look: Students draw strip diagrams, mark the unknown with a question mark, and explain whether it is a part or the whole.

assess: Which part of the story is unknown?
How did your strip diagram help you choose to add or subtract?
advance: Can you change the story so the start is unknown?
Can you write two number sentences that match your strip diagram?

assess: Point to the unknown in your drawing.
Is the unknown a part or the whole?
advance: Can you solve it by counting up on a number line?
What number sentence matches your drawing?

assess: What do we know in this story?
What are we trying to find?
advance: Let's act it out with counters. How many are hiding?
Is the cup holding the start or the end?
support: Use numbers within 20 first with the same story types.
Give a strip diagram with the whole and parts already labeled.

stems: I solved it by ___ and checked by ___.
d: Represent and solve addition and subtraction word problems where unknowns may be any one of the terms in the problem.

mis.m: Draws 4 lines that do not all meet and calls it a quadrilateral.
mis.why: Students do not yet know that a polygon must be closed with sides meeting at vertices.
mis.fix: Build shapes with straws and connectors or on geoboards, and check that every end meets another end.

mis.m: Counts a side twice or mixes up sides and vertices, saying a triangle has 6 sides.
mis.why: The words side and vertex are new and students count around without a starting mark.
mis.fix: Trace each side with a finger while counting, then put a sticker or dot on each vertex and count again.

mis.m: Will not call a tilted or long thin shape a triangle or hexagon.
mis.why: Students have mostly seen shapes in one position and size.
mis.fix: Turn and stretch shapes on a geoboard and ask, 'How many sides and vertices now? Is it still the same kind of shape?'

cra.c: Students build shapes with geoboards, straws and connectors, or craft sticks to match attribute cards such as '5 sides and 5 vertices'.
cra.r: Students draw shapes on dot paper to match given attributes, marking each vertex with a dot and numbering each side.
cra.a: Students name and describe shapes by attributes: 'This is a pentagon because it has 5 sides and 5 vertices.'
cra.look: Students build and draw shapes from attribute cards and count sides and vertices aloud while pointing.

assess: How did you make sure your shape has 5 vertices?
Why is your shape a hexagon?
advance: Can you make a different-looking shape with the same number of sides?
Can you make a shape where the number of sides and vertices are not the same? Why not?

assess: Show me each vertex on your drawing.
How many sides did you count?
advance: Can you draw the same kind of shape another way?
What shape would you have if you added one more side?

assess: Point to a side. Point to a vertex.
Do all the sides meet?
advance: Count the sides with me while you trace them.
Put a dot on each corner. How many dots?
support: Use a geoboard with a model shape to copy first.
Give an attribute card with pictures of a side and a vertex.

stems: My shape has ___ sides and ___ vertices.
d: Create two-dimensional shapes based on given attributes, including number of sides and vertices.
